newsitem.title: USA: Heinz cutting 2,500 jobs, closing 25 plants.
newsitem.headline: Heinz cutting 2,500 jobs, closing 25 plants.

text.p: H.J. Heinz Co. unveiled its long-awaited restructuring plan Friday, saying it will close or sell at least 25 plants, cut 2,500 jobs worldwide and take a $650 million pre-tax charge to cover the costs.
The company, which produces a wide variety of food products besides its famous condiments, said it expected the measures to result in pre-tax savings of about $120 million next year.

The Pittsburgh-based global food marketer told a financial analysts meeting in San Francisco that it will exit at least four "non-strategic" businesses as part of the reorganization, the biggest in its history.
Heinz said its intention was to focus on expanding its global leadership in high-margin ketchup and condiments, tuna products and weight-control and other prepackaged foods.

The company, whose brands include Heinz, StarKist, Ore-Ida, 9-Lives, Weight Watchers, Budget Gourmet, Earth's Best and Ken-L Ration, said one of the first steps in the reorganization was the sale of its Ore-Ida's food business to McCain Foods Ltd of Canada for $500 million.
It added that it expected that cash proceeds from all the asset sales it contemplates over the next 12 months should realise between $750 million to $850 million.
The company said that, in all, it will close or sell at least 25 other plants throughout the world.
In addition, the company will reduce its global workforce by 2,500 employees, or about 6 percent.

"We regret the loss of jobs but this plan is necessary to make us more competitive in the tough global marketplace," Chairman and Chief Executive Anthony J. F. O'Reilly told a meeting of the Security Analysts of San Francisco.
He added that the specific plants and businesses to be closed will not be publicly identified until after affected employees have been notified in the next few months.

O'Reilly said the goals of the sweeping makeover included ensuring at least 10 percent earnings growth into the next century and increasing sales to between $14 billion and $15 billion by 2003, compared with $9.5 billion this year.
He also said the company intended to greatly increase its overseas sales from their current level of 43 percent of annual revenues.
"The overseas growth will stem from rapid expansion into the fast-growing markets of eastern Europe, Asia, the Indian sub-continent and South America," O'Reilly said.
Separately Friday Heinz announced record results for its fiscal third quarter.
It said its net income climbed to $174.4 million, or 47 cents a share, from $156.5 million, or 42 cents a share, as revenues expanded to $2.31 billion from $2.19 billion.
The earnings-per-share figure was exactly in line with Wall Street forecasts, according to First Call, which tracks analysts' estimates.
Heinz's stock added 12.5 cents to $41.875 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
